_readme: Reproducibility is scored as SLOTS, not as a fixed list of field names.
A slot is one decision somebody re-running this evaluation has to be able to
pin down. Any one of its `satisfied_by` paths satisfies it, so a study that
discloses `token_limit` is credited the same as one disclosing `max_tokens`.

Paths under generation_config.additional_details are where most sources actually put their setup — temperature_raw, effort, repeats, eval_split, lm_eval_task and so on. Check there first when a source looks undocumented.

Harness is deliberately TWO slots: `harness` (which one) and `harness_pin` (which version/task config of it). Collapsing them would let a library name alone — present on 99% of rows — stand for reproducibility.
EDITING THIS FILE
- Add a field to a slot: append its path to `satisfied_by`. No code change.
- Add a slot: append an object with id/label/hint/satisfied_by/applies.
- Retire a slot: delete it, or set `applies` to "never".
Paths resolve against the normalised evidence object built by
lib/reproducibility-slots.ts (see EVIDENCE_SHAPE there). Unknown paths are
ignored rather than throwing, so a typo costs you credit, not a crash.
APPLICABILITY
`applies` names a rule implemented in lib/reproducibility-slots.ts:
always              - every run must disclose this
reasoning_run       - only when the run used a reasoning/thinking budget
sampling_controlled - every run except one scored from log-probabilities,
where nothing is sampled and there is no setting to
state
generative_run      - every run except one scored from log-probabilities,
which generates nothing and so has no length to limit
agentic_run         - only when the run used a tool-using scaffold
never               - retired; keeps the slot visible in this file as history
A slot that does not apply is shown as `n/a` and LEAVES THE DENOMINATOR.
A slot whose applicability cannot be determined is shown as `unknown` and
also leaves the denominator: absence of a knob must never read as absence
of rigour. What counts as absence is deliberately narrow. Only an
affirmative log-prob classification retires the decoding and length slots;
a run whose scoring mode nobody recorded is still asked for both, because
an undisclosed setting is the thing this score exists to measure.
Score = disclosed / applicable. Surfaces should show both numbers, because a
variable denominator makes a bare percentage hard to compare across pages.
DEFINED BUT NOT SCORED: `prompt_format` and `model_build` (applies="never").
Both genuinely change a score — few-shot count, chat template, dtype and
revision all move numbers, on generative runs as much as on log-prob ones.
They are off because almost nothing in the corpus reports them, so switching
them on marks nearly every page down at once. Flip `applies` to "always" when
you want that; the swissai_apertus_evals records are the template for what a
source that does report them looks like (output_type, lm_eval_task,
num_fewshot, fewshot_as_multiturn, chat_template_sha, prompt_template).
NOT SCORED: `scoring_variant` (raw vs length-normalised accuracy). It is a
real ambiguity — the two differ by a median of 3.3 points on the same
log-prob run — but it cannot be READ from what sources report. HF Open LLM
v2 records a metric id of "accuracy" for every task including the
normalised ones, so the slot was being satisfied by a label that does not
disambiguate: crediting a non-disclosure, which is worse than the penalty
it was meant to avoid. Penalising instead would mark sources down for a
distinction they may well have made and simply not spelled out.
This belongs in the METRIC REGISTRY, not in a reproducibility checklist:
`accuracy` and `normalized_accuracy` should be distinct canonical metrics
(swissai-apertus-evals already reports them separately), at which point the
variant is carried by the metric id itself and needs no slot here.
NOT SCORED (on purpose): `standard_error`, `confidence_interval` and the
other uncertainty statistics. They tell a reader how much to trust the
number, which matters — but they are not inputs somebody needs in order to
re-run the evaluation, and reproducibility is about re-running it. They
surface under "Also reported".
NOT SCORED (on purpose): `prompt_template` and `num_few_shot` are reported
by some sources and show up under "Also reported" in the per-row panel. They
are a real reproducibility input, but only 414 of 83,842 rows carry a prompt
template, so scoring them today would mark almost every page down for one
field. Add a `prompting` slot here when the corpus supports it.
SCOPE NOTE: `attempts` is currently scored only for agentic runs. Repeat
count arguably matters for every evaluation; widening it to "always" is a
one-word edit here, but it adds a slot almost nothing in the corpus
discloses, so every page's score would drop. Decide that deliberately.

slots.label: Decoding
slots.hint: Sampling controls a re-runner has to match. Absent by nature only on log-prob scoring, where nothing is sampled.

slots.label: Reasoning budget
slots.hint: How much thinking the model was allowed before answering.

slots.label: Length limit
slots.hint: Where generation was cut off — tokens, messages or steps. A log-prob run generates nothing, so it has no length limit to state.

slots.label: Harness
slots.hint: WHICH scaffold, agent or eval library produced the run — named, so somebody can obtain it. A property of the harness is not its identity: `compaction: off` says nothing about what you would have to install.

slots.label: Harness version
slots.hint: Which version or task config of that harness. `eval_library` is populated on 99% of rows, so naming the library alone would hand almost every page a free slot — but "lm-evaluation-harness" without a version or task id is not something you can re-run.

slots.label: Context handling
slots.hint: What happened when the transcript outgrew the window — compaction, truncation, or nothing.

slots.label: Test set
slots.hint: Which items the score covers: an item count, a split or a subset. Any one of them satisfies the slot, because a score over 7 tasks and one over 86 are not the same measurement.

slots.label: Attempts
slots.hint: How many times the evaluation was run — repeated trajectories, epochs or samples the reported score pools over. Not the number of tasks.

slots.label: Scoring variant
slots.hint: Raw vs length-normalised accuracy. On the same log-prob run the two differ by a median of 3.3 points — but most sources report a metric id of plain "accuracy" for both, so we cannot tell which we are looking at.

slots.label: Prompt format
slots.hint: The prompt and answer-choice templates (doc_to_text / doc_to_choice), few-shot count, and whether a chat template was applied. Chat template alone moves MMLU-Pro by up to 3.6 points.

slots.label: Model build
slots.hint: Which weights exactly — revision/commit and numeric precision. Two runs of 'the same model' at different dtype are not the same run.

_readme: Evidence used by the named rules above.
SCORING MODE is the first question, because it decides which knobs exist at
all, and `canonical_paths` is read before anything else: it holds the
producer's own `scoring_mode` column, whose only meaningful values are
`generative` and `log_prob`. Anything else, including a null on a row the
producer could not classify, falls through to the heuristics below, so a
snapshot without the column is scored exactly as it was before it existed.
About 25% of the corpus (~19k of 78k triples) is scored from
LOG-PROBABILITIES rather than generated text: the harness scores the model's
likelihood over fixed answer choices and nothing is sampled. Those runs have
no temperature and no max_tokens, so the old rule could never pass them and
counted every one as a gap.
Detect it from `output_type` (multiple_choice / loglikelihood /
loglikelihood_rolling are log-prob; generate_until is generative), or from a
reward model's `model_type`. NEVER infer it from the benchmark name — helm_*
does multiple choice by generating the answer letter, which is generative.
Where it lives today: swissai_apertus_evals puts output_type in
generation_config.additional_details; reward-bench puts model_type in
model_info.additional_details. HF Open LLM v2 (~19k rows) does NOT carry it in
the EEE record at all — it is only in the harness dumps
(open-llm-leaderboard/results, configs[<task>].output_type), so those rows
resolve to UNKNOWN mode. Unknown does NOT excuse them: their decoding and
length slots still apply and read as undisclosed, because nothing on the row
rules the knobs out. The producer's `scoring_mode` column is what turns those
rows into a real n/a, and it is read first.
`reasoning_markers` decide whether a run was a reasoning run; when none are
present the run's type is UNKNOWN, not 'not reasoning' — the registry carries
no reasoning flag today (checked 2026-09-21: canonical_models.tags/metadata
hold HF pipeline tags, licences and download counts only).
A marker only counts when its value is AFFIRMATIVE. `reasoning: false` and
`reasoning_effort: "none"` are disclosures, and they are credited as such,
but what they disclose is that the run did no thinking, so they cannot be
the evidence that it did, and they open no other slot that depends on the
run having reasoned. A slot the source answered stays in the denominator
whatever the answer was: `compaction: false` is context handling, stated.
Being a reasoning run does not retire the decoding slot. Which APIs accept
which sampling parameters is a capability fact about a model, and nothing
here carries it; asserting it from a row would invent the fact. Add
`supports_temperature` upstream in evaleval/entity-registry-data and this
could be decided from the model rather than guessed.
